problem.text: Everyday at school, Jo climbs a flight of $6$ stairs. Jo can take the stairs $1$, $2$, or $3$ at a time. For example, Jo could climb $3$, then $1$, then $2$. In how many ways can Jo climb the stairs?

steps.title: Where to start: look at Jo's last move
steps.body: Listing every way to climb $6$ stairs is easy to get wrong. The clue is that each move is only $1$, $2$ or $3$ stairs, so any climb to the top ends with one of just three possible last moves. Let $a_n$ be the number of ways to climb $n$ stairs, and try to build $a_n$ from smaller cases.

your_turn.prompt: If Jo's last move to reach stair $n$ is $2$ stairs, where was Jo just before that move?
your_turn.answer: On stair $n-2$. Any way of reaching stair $n-2$ can be finished with that one $2$-stair move.

steps.title: Write the recursion and the first values
steps.body:
The last move is $1$, $2$ or $3$ stairs, so Jo came from stair $n-1$, $n-2$ or $n-3$. Climbs with different last moves are different, so no climb is counted twice:
$$a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2} + a_{n-3}$$
For small $n$ just list the climbs: $a_1 = 1$ and $a_2 = 2$ (either $1,1$ or $2$).

your_turn.prompt: List all the ways to climb $3$ stairs. What is $a_3$?

steps.title: Build up one stair at a time
steps.body: Now use the recursion, always adding the three values just before. Careful: it is easy to forget the $3$-stair move and add only the two previous values. That is the Fibonacci rule from the previous example, and it undercounts here.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Next $a_5 = 7 + 4 + 2 = 13$, and then $a_6 = a_5 + a_4 + a_3 = 13 + 7 + 4 = 24$. So Jo can climb the $6$ stairs in $24$ ways. The answer is **(E)**.

wrong_choices.A: This is the count if Jo could only take $1$ or $2$ stairs at a time (the Fibonacci rule $a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}$ gives $1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13$). The $3$-stair move adds more ways.
